case_study_insert.main_stem: Voltwise Renewable Energy (VRE) is a public limited company in the renewable energy sector, installing rooftop solar panels and battery storage for commercial clients, with a workforce of 50. Founded in 2013 by Daniel Okafor, VRE operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership and prides itself on rapid installation. VRE plans to invest $1,200,000 in a solar-panel recycling and battery-storage facility, financed by a $700,000 ten-year bank loan and a $500,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $20.00 a unit and a selling price of $32.00, and currently produces 80,000 units a year. A skills gap in battery-storage technicians and a rising installation defect rate are delaying projects and threatening VRE's growth.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q2 2025: VRE installed 6,400 solar units last quarter, with an installation defect rate of 3.2%, up from 1.9% a year earlier. Customer complaints rose from 19 to 34 a month, and average installation time lengthened to 6.5 days. A survey of 300 commercial clients found that 71% value certified battery-storage technicians and 62% would pay a 4% premium for faster installation. Technician records show 12 of 50 staff lack battery-storage accreditation; on-the-job training is offered internally, while off-the-job courses at the technical college cost $1,100 per technician.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Voltwise Renewable Energy for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (December 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, increasing debt-service costs for VRE's $700,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.50 to $14.34 an hour, lifting the cost of installation crews. (3) Solar panel and lithium-cell input costs have risen 11.8% year-on-year, while energy-sector inflation is 7.4% and commercial demand for rooftop solar grew 5.1%.

questions.question_text: VRE has funded its expansion partly with a $700,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for VRE of raising the $500,000 balance through a share issue rather than more borrowing.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue does not have to be repaid and creates no regular interest charge, which protects VRE's cash flow while it services the $700,000 ten-year bank loan and carries fixed costs of $480,000 a year. Equity funding of $500,000 therefore leaves more cash to spend on the $1,200,000 recycling and battery-storage facility and on the skilled technicians needed to close the skills gap, without diverting money into interest payments that would shrink the $12.00 contribution earned on each of the 80,000 units.

Point 2: Equity also strengthens the balance sheet and lowers financial risk. As a public limited company, VRE can issue shares to spread ownership, reducing dependence on a lender that might impose covenants or, after the base-rate rise to 5.25%, make borrowing more expensive. With no new debt to service, the firm is better placed to withstand delays caused by the 3.2% installation defect rate and to invest in extra training. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders' control and possible dividend expectations, but for a growth-oriented energy business facing rising installation demand this is a sustainable way to fund expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over further borrowing (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to VRE's expansion, financing and skills needs.

questions.question_text: VRE is launching its new solar-panel recycling facility. Consider trade journal advertising, sponsoring an industry conference, or social media marketing. Which should VRE choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade journal advertising: Adverts in renewable-energy and facilities-management journals reach exactly the commercial clients who commission rooftop solar and battery storage, at a controlled cost for a 50-employee firm funding a $1,200,000 facility. Detailed technical messages about recycling and certified installation can be included, which suits the 71% of 300 surveyed clients who value accredited technicians. However, journals have long lead times and limited reach, so they may not build broad awareness quickly enough.

Sponsoring an industry conference: This puts VRE in front of senior buyers and project engineers in person, allowing demonstrations of the new facility and immediate networking, with strong credibility in a technical market. It is expensive, however, relative to VRE's $700,000 loan commitment, and impact is confined to one event and its attendees, so the message may fade once the conference ends and it does not reach the wider 62% of clients who would pay a 4% premium for speed.

Social media marketing: Targeted campaigns can show the falling installation times, the recycling story and technician accreditation to a broad audience cheaply, with measurable engagement and rapid updates. Conversion into large commercial contracts can be slow, and content must be sustained, but cost per contact is low and results are trackable.

Recommendation: VRE should choose trade journal advertising as the primary channel, reinforced by social media. Journals reach the technical buyers who decide contracts and can carry the accreditation message that 71% of clients demand, at a cost that fits alongside the $700,000 loan. Conference sponsorship is rejected as too expensive and short-lived for a business with a skills gap and 3.2% defect rate to fix; social media alone is rejected because it rarely closes large commercial tenders, so it should support rather than replace the trade campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal reference to VRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to VRE and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in VRE's context with a clear, justified recommendation explaining why the conference and social-media-only options are rejected.

questions.question_text: VRE's skills gap and 3.2% installation defect rate are delaying projects. Explain two benefits for VRE of using democratic leadership with its technicians.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership invites VRE's 50 technicians to contribute ideas on installation methods and battery-storage procedures, which can directly reduce the 3.2% defect rate and the rise in complaints from 19 to 34 a month. Because the firm uses a flat organisational structure, technicians can raise problems quickly with founder Daniel Okafor, so faults found on site are fed back into practice and the 6.5-day installation time can be shortened, helping satisfy the 62% of clients who would pay a 4% premium for faster work.

Point 2: Consulting technicians also helps close the skills gap and retain scarce expertise. When the 12 staff lacking battery-storage accreditation are involved in planning their own development, they are more motivated to train, so the $1,100 per-technician courses are more effective. A participative style gives skilled workers autonomy and recognition, reducing the likelihood that they leave for competitors, which protects the knowledgeable workforce VRE needs to deliver the $1,200,000 recycling and storage facility on schedule.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of democratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to VRE's skills gap, defect rate and client data.

questions.question_text: VRE must uplift the skills of technicians for the new battery-storage facility. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the technical college. Which should VRE choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching at VRE's own installations is directly relevant to its solar and battery systems, costs no fees, and keeps technicians working while they learn, protecting the 6,400 units installed last quarter. Experienced staff can demonstrate the exact routines that cause the 3.2% defect rate, so improvements are immediate and tailored. The limitations are that trainers are productive technicians whose own work slows, bad habits may be passed on, and there is no independent certificate, which matters because 71% of clients value certified technicians.

Off-the-job courses: The technical college charges $1,100 per technician, so accrediting the 12 staff who lack battery-storage accreditation would cost $13,200 (12 × $1,100) — small beside the $1,200,000 facility. Courses offer structured, up-to-date content and a recognised certificate that directly answers the 71% of surveyed clients who value accreditation, supporting the 4% premium opportunity. However, technicians are away from projects, lengthening the current 6.5-day installation time, and generic teaching may not match VRE's equipment.

Decision: VRE should choose off-the-job courses for the 12 technicians needing accreditation, followed by on-the-job coaching. The certificate directly meets the stated preference of 71% of clients and costs only $13,200, whereas on-the-job training alone is rejected because it cannot provide the formal accreditation those clients demand and may take longer to reduce the 3.2% defect rate. The college route also creates a portable record that supports tendering after the $1,200,000 facility opens and helps retain staff who value recognised qualifications, easing the skills gap. To limit disruption to the 6,400-unit quarterly workload, VRE should stagger the 12 places rather than send everyone at once, and pair each course with depot coaching so generic content is translated into VRE's own routines.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both methods with reference to VRE's costs and client requirements.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in VRE's context with a justified decision covering accreditation, cost and disruption.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VRE's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($32.00 − $20.00) = $480,000 ÷ $12.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $32.00 − $20.00 = $12.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $12.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VRE's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing break-even output of 40,000 units with actual output of 80,000 units gives a margin of safety of 40,000 units, showing a large buffer and supporting investment in the $1,200,000 recycling facility.
2. Contribution of $12.00 a unit lets managers test pricing: the 4% premium sought by 62% of clients would add about $1.28 per unit at the $32.00 price, lifting contribution to roughly $13.28 and lowering break-even output below 40,000 units.
3. With fixed costs of $480,000, managers can set the volume needed to service the $700,000 loan and check that the 6,400 units installed per quarter can be sustained while the skills gap persists.
4. Unit cost of $26.00 ($480,000 ÷ 80,000 units = $6.00 fixed cost per unit, plus $20.00 variable cost) can be tracked against the 11.8% panel and lithium-cell inflation, while labour productivity of 80,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,600 units per worker helps judge whether the 3.2% defect rate is being tackled efficiently.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $12.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 40,000 units vs 80,000 output; premium-pricing modelling vs $480,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume target; and unit-cost benchmarking at $26.00 with productivity of 1,600 units per worker.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VRE's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VRE's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 35.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 16.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue of $8,000,000 in 2024 less cost of sales of $5,600,000 gives gross profit of $2,400,000; revenue of $9,000,000 in 2025 less $5,850,000 gives $3,150,000. Gross profit divided by revenue yields 30.0% and 35.0%. Operating profit of $1,000,000 in 2024 and $1,440,000 in 2025, each divided by revenue, yields 12.5% and 16.0%. Operating profit divided by capital employed of $5,000,000 and $6,000,000 yields 20.0% and 24.0%.

Evaluation: Each measure improved strongly. The first margin rose from 30.0% to 35.0%, meaning VRE retained more of each sales dollar after direct costs even though input costs were rising, which is consistent with the 4% premium some clients accept and with better control of the 80,000 units installed. The overall margin climbed from 12.5% to 16.0%, so overheads were absorbed more effectively as revenue grew by $1,000,000 despite the skills gap and installation delays. The return on capital moved from 20.0% to 24.0%; although capital employed rose to $6,000,000 to fund the new facility, operating profit grew faster, so the investment is already earning a better return. Interest payable actually fell from $200,000 to $190,000, easing the pressure from the $700,000 loan and the higher base rate.

Conclusion: VRE's profitability has improved. All three ratios moved favourably at the same time, and the gain is not explained by higher borrowing or asset sales, since interest fell and capital was used more efficiently. The main risk is that the 11.8% rise in panel and lithium-cell costs and the 6.2% wage rise could erode margins next year, so management should protect the premium and close the skills gap quickly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes with little or no accurate calculation.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Correctly calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratios for both years with detailed evaluation of margins, capital efficiency and financing and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VRE of requiring battery-storage accreditation for its technicians.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Requiring accreditation directly addresses the skills gap and the 71% of 300 surveyed commercial clients who value certified battery-storage technicians. It gives VRE a credible basis for charging the 4% premium that 62% of clients would accept for faster, assured installation, helping protect the $12.00 contribution per unit against 11.8% input-cost inflation and differentiate the business when tendering for contracts after the $1,200,000 facility opens.

Disadvantage: Accreditation is costly and slow. The insert states off-the-job courses cost $1,100 per technician and that 12 of 50 staff are not yet accredited, so achieving full coverage requires a real training budget and time away from the 6,400 units installed each quarter, which may lengthen the current 6.5-day installation time. The insert gives no breakdown of VRE's $20.00 variable cost, so the payback cannot be quantified precisely, and stricter entry rules could also delay recruitment during a skills shortage. Rivals without the requirement could undercut VRE on price and win the 38% (100% − 62%) of clients who are not prepared to pay the 4% premium, so the policy must be backed by the faster installation that underpins that premium.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development using VRE's survey, costs and skills data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 11.8% rise in solar panel and lithium-cell costs will affect VRE. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): If VRE's $700,000 loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $700,000 = $5,250 a year (0.0075 × $700,000). Against fixed costs of $480,000 this is modest, and a share issue has already funded $500,000 of the $1,200,000 facility, limiting new borrowing. Higher base rates may still raise the cost of future debt and cool commercial investment in rooftop solar, but VRE can cap the effect by fixing the rate, so this is a controllable, relatively small pressure.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.34 an hour): Installation crews are likely to be hourly paid, so the rise pushes up the cost of the 6,400 units installed each quarter. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so a defensible annual wage total cannot be invented; the sound comparison is with given productivity of 80,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,600 units per worker. If output per technician holds, the rise is bearable; if the skills gap and 3.2% defect rate reduce output, unit labour cost rises and the $12.00 contribution per unit falls.

Input cost inflation (11.8% panels and lithium cells): The $20.00 variable cost per unit is affected by these inputs, but the insert does not decompose it, so only an explicit bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 11.8%, that would add 11.8% × $20.00 = $2.36 per unit, and over 80,000 units that is $188,800 a year (80,000 × $2.36) — several times the interest effect. Even a $1.00-per-unit increase would cost $80,000 a year. VRE can offset part of this through the 4% premium and the 62% of clients who would pay it.

Conclusion: The 11.8% rise in solar panel and lithium-cell costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every unit, directly attacks the $12.00 contribution that supports the $1,200,000 investment, and is broadly beyond VRE's short-term control. The interest rise is small and hedgeable, and the wage rise is serious but depends on unstated hours and on productivity VRE can influence, so both rank below input inflation.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to VRE.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on VRE's costs, financing or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
